blocks.text: The Midrash passage (Rabba Bereschit fol. 24b) is zoologically interesting. The garments of skins (כותנות עור) which Adam and Eve had made for themselves were said to have been either איגיאה, or אנגיה, or לגאי, or סיסרטון, or גלא קסינון, or צמר גמלים, or finally צמר ארנבין. Evidently the skins of various animals are meant here. איגיאה is, as Buxdorf (Lex. 21) conjectures, αἰγεία [aigeia], of goats; אנגיה I take to be derived from anguis, snake, since a passage was already cited in §. 288, note, according to which those garments were said to have consisted of snakeskin; לגאי, Buxdorf (l. c. p. 1122) conjectures, is the Greek λαγεία [lageia], of hares; סיסרטון, for which the Aruch reads סיסרנון, is the Greek σισύρνα [sisyrna], goat leather; גלא קסינון I take to be γαλῆ [galē], weasel; the addition קסינון means small, [p. 367] cf. §. 123, the same as גלאקטין*). The last two opinions take not skins but wool, or hair, to be the material of those garments.

We give here once more an overview of all the animals mentioned in both Talmuds and in the Midrash (Rabba), in which the different varieties of some species have been counted separately. There are in all 365 kinds of animals, which are divided into the following species: 75 mammals, 88 birds, 24 amphibians, 46 fishes, 8 molluscs, 81 insects, 25 worms, 7 zoophytes and 11 fabulous animals.
General numerical proportions regarding the number of animals have been given in §. 12.
[p. 368] Appendix.

Whereas so far, from the Jerusalem Talm. and the Midrash, such natural-historical material has been communicated at the relevant places as seemed necessary to supplement the statements made by the Babylonian Talmud, here those animal species shall follow separately which are mentioned only in those two sources first named, likewise the animal names that are found only in them. But since both, the species as well as the names, are not especially numerous, we give them alphabetically without a scientific-systematic classification. It should be noted that only the Cracow edition (of the year 1609) of the Jerusalem Talmud, which is unfortunately very incorrect, was available to us; we will therefore gladly expect and accept corrections from those who have access to correct editions of that Talmud furnished with commentaries.

אבחטם, thus Kilajim ch. 8, Hal. 3, but for which Sabbat C. 5, fol. 7b has: אמכטם; in both passages the Talmud explains the word by חמר סלק, which perhaps means "Seleucid ass." The biblical אשור (Gen. 2, 14) is explained by the Talm. (Babylonian Ketuboth 10b) by סליקא, and the asses in that region may have been distinguished by their size.

אוז הים (Kilajim C. 8. H. 6), or אוז ים (B. Kama C. 4. H. 10), the goose of the sea. It may not be paired with the domestic goose (אוז יישוב l. c.). By the former perhaps the pelican may be meant, which even now is called by some: crop goose, or sea goose.

[p. 369] אורדען (Rabba Wajikra f. 190a), instead of which the parallel passage (Bereschit f. 12b) has עורדען, frog, which carried a scorpion across a river. In the Babylonian Talm. (Nedarim 41a) קרוקתא stands for it, on which see §. 271.

אספרון, Babba (Bereschit fol. 9, 2) says: "One may not tie the fish מירן together with the fish אספרון and let them be drawn along thus in the water, because it is a mixing of kinds (כלאים)." Instead of this, the Jalkut (Schimoni Bereschit fol. 4b) has שני דגים חד אוכם וחד חיור "a black and a white fish"; and the Jerusalem Talmud (Kilajim C. 1. H. 6): "One should not lead fishes on a thread which is attached to the ear of the לכיסא (λευκὸς [leukos], white) and to the ear of the יריקא (green, §. 201) fish; thus some also wanted to explain מירן and אספרון as colours and to interpret מירן as black (perhaps from ἀμαυρὸν [amauron]; on the aphoristic α [a] see §. 511), אספרון as white; the author of the Matnat Kehuna explains the words in the op-
posite way, according to which אספרון means black and מירן white.
Finally Buxdorf (Lex. p. 172) cites Guil. Postellus, who in the Latin translation of the Midrash renders מירן by Miaron and אספרון by Asporon, thus as animal names.

Since אספרון as a colour cannot be documented from Greek, two fish names are in fact more likely to be conjectured here, perhaps the Μύρινος [Myrinos] and the Σφύραινα [Sphyraina], cf. §. 341; both are sea fishes; cf. Aristot. (Thiergesch. 8, 20, 6, and 9, 3, 1).

ארי נמירון (Rabba Bereschit 86, d); in earlier editions אריה אימרון stands; the first reading means leopard, since the Latin and German word, and likewise the Aramaic, is composed of two parts, the latter of ארי, lion, and נמר, pard.

The second reading means the tamed lion (like ἥμερος [hēmeros]), as opposed to the כלב אגריון, wild (like ἄγριος [agrios]) dog. This passage speaks of the mating of the wild dog with the ארי נמירון; at least it is known that the tiger sometimes mates with the dog, see Aristot. (Thiergesch. 8, 27, 8).
בן הפילים (Rabba Schemoth f. 133b) stands for בן נפילים (skink), which was discussed in §. 277.
בר הריה (Rabba Wajikra fol. 170b) for ריה (vulture), on which cf. §. 196.
בר נש דטור (Jerusalem Talmud Kilajim C. 8. fol. 31, c) as a designation of the fabulously depicted animal אבני שדה, cf. §. 111.
[p. 370] גורי פרסיא (Persian lions) Jerusalem Talmud B. batra C. 2, H. 3; f. p. 71 note *.

גלאקטינון. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Sabbat C. 2, fol. 4, d) there are three opinions on the identification of the Tachash animal (§. 176); according to the first it was a kind of colour טיינין (by which Midr. Rabba Ester fol. 120, d explains חכלח; as is well known, the LXX explain it in a similar sense, see §. 176); according to the second it was the unclean animal גלאקטינון; according to the third it was a clean animal.

In Midr. Rabba Kohelet fol. 85, d there stands (probably incorrectly) אלטינין for טיינין and גלטינין for גלאקטינון; this latter word designates either the small weasel or the sable, on which cf. §. 521.
